sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for? No.** The title at the top, "Winter timetable at the harbour" (about x 120–715, y 60–100), promises a timetable. The two columns below it hold only prose about opening hours, how often boats run, the waiting room and what can come on board. There is not one departure time. The only schedule fact is "every ninety minutes", and it is buried mid-paragraph in the left column at about y 295. A passenger who comes to find out when the next boat leaves can't answer that from this page. They have to read every paragraph to learn the answer isn't here. That is the opposite of a page that explains itself at a glance (Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*; Nielsen 8, every element supports the main task). **Defect. Major.** Fix: either add the timetable itself (first and last sailing, departure times, perhaps as a short table under the title) and make it the dominant element, or retitle the page to say what it actually is, such as general winter information for passengers.

2. **Does each heading name what its section holds? No.** The only subheading, "Fares and cards" at the top of the right column (x 680, y 135–160), sits over text about crossing times in different winds, bicycles, prams and wheelchairs, and dogs. Nothing in it is about fares or cards. The season card is actually mentioned in the left column at about y 226. A reader looking for prices follows the heading, finds none, and starts to distrust the rest of the page's labels (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6, Headings and labels). **Defect. Major.** Fix: retitle the section to match what it holds (crossings, and what you can bring on board), or move the fare and card content under it. Prices are what passengers act on, so if fares belong on this page they need a section that actually holds them.

3. **Does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears? No.** The two columns are the same kind of block: equal 480 px measures, the same body type and the same closing rule. But the right column opens with a bold subheading and the left starts straight into body text at y 135. The left column reads as an introduction to the right one, or as a block whose heading went missing. The tops of the two columns also don't line up: the left starts with body text at y 145, the right with its heading at y 147, so their first lines of body text start about 40 px apart. That breaks the pattern the matching columns set (Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*, "Repeated elements follow one program"; Nielsen 4). **Convention. Minor.** Fix: give the left column a heading of the same style that names its content (for example, office hours and sailings), or drop the subheading and let both columns run as plain text.

4. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something? No.** Each column ends with a thin grey rule across its full width at y ≈ 585. Below the rules there is nothing but about 215 px of white space to the bottom of the image. The rules separate the text from emptiness, so they look like dividers left over from a template, or like the end of a page that should carry on. They also sit about 75 px below the left text and about 115 px below the right, which makes the uneven column lengths more obvious (Tufte, non-data ink; Lupton; "No rules, boxes, or ornament where space would do"). **Taste or convention. Minor.** Fix: remove the rules, or, if something follows them on the full page (such as a footer or the missing timetable), close the gap so the rules visibly introduce it.

**What's working.**
- Every element uses the same serif family and the same near-black ink on white, at three sizes in a calm, plain arrangement. It reads as one sober public notice, which suits a harbour office, and there are no mismatched parts.
- The copy is finished and well written: complete sentences, concrete facts ("twenty minutes and a rough one closer to thirty-five"), no placeholder text and no typos.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the band below the rules is the true end of the page, or a timetable or footer that hadn't rendered when the screenshot was taken. Check this in a live browser. If a timetable does appear there, finding 1 shrinks to "the timetable sits below a fold and below the prose".

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 4 yes, 4 no (purpose clear in one sentence; every element does a job; same kind of element looks the same; headings name their content), 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None. All three checklist lines are yes. Two hierarchy problems that no checklist line covers are below, for the director to weigh.

1. *(Off the checklist: the levels don't match across the two columns.)* The right column opens with a bold heading, "Fares and cards" (~680,135–160). The left column has no heading. Its first body paragraph starts at the same height (y≈145), so body text in one column lines up with a heading in the other. A viewer scanning for a topic finds only one label on the page. The left column's content (opening hours, sailings every ninety minutes, the waiting room) has nothing to scan by, even though it is the "timetable" the title promises. "Fares and cards" also reads as if it heads the whole lower half, or sits one level above the left text. The fix: give the left column its own heading at the same level, such as hours and sailings, so both columns share one structure. Or drop to a single column with headings in sequence. Defect (common sense, no catalog entry). Weight: major, because on a page people scan for practical facts, the headings are the only way in.
2. *(Off the checklist: the heading promises something the section doesn't deliver.)* "Fares and cards" (~680,147) sits over paragraphs about crossing times, bicycles, prams and dogs. None of them mentions a fare. The season card appears in the *left* column (y≈226). A viewer who scans to this heading for prices finds none and has to read everything to learn that the page has no fares on it. The fix: retitle the section after what it covers, such as "On board" or "The crossing". Or move the fares and the season-card text under it. Defect (copy, common sense). Weight: major for anyone who came for prices, which is one of the most likely reasons to visit this page.

**What's working.**
- The title (~120,60–100) is clearly the largest and heaviest thing on the page. It is bold serif at roughly twice the body size, so the eye always knows where to start and what the page is about.
- "Fares and cards" differs from the body text in both size (~22 vs ~18 px, by eye) and weight (bold vs regular). The size step is small, but the bold makes it read as a heading at a glance (Dair's "obvious contrast" holds through weight). Keep the weight contrast if more headings are added.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines? No.** The left column's body starts at about y=145. The right column's body starts at about y=184, under "Fares and cards". That is a 39 px shift on what looks like a 27 px line spacing, so the two columns are out of step all the way down. Paragraph 2 nearly lines up (left about y=294, right about y=292) and then drifts apart again. Across the gutter the lines sit between each other, so the page looks slightly unsettled, and the near-hit at paragraph 2 looks like a mistake rather than a choice. The rule is that lines in neighboring columns share baselines (`references/typography.md`, "Lines of text align across columns"; I couldn't open the entry, so I'm not giving a source). Fix: make the heading plus the gap below it take a whole number of lines (54 px here), so the right body lands on the left column's lines. Another way is to give the left column a heading of the same height, which also fixes finding 2. Kind: convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Do only related elements look alike, with no accidental groups? No.** The two columns are the same width and look like matching sections, but only the right one has a heading, at 680,147. The left column (120–600, y=145–497) has none. A reader can't tell whether the left text is an intro under the page title or a section whose heading is missing. The copy makes this worse. The season-card paragraph (left, about y=226–253) is the only text about "cards", but it sits away from the "Fares and cards" heading. The text under that heading talks about crossing times, bicycles, prams and dogs, and gives no fares. A passenger looking for fares goes to the labelled section and doesn't find them. This is common sense, with no catalog entry beyond Gestalt similarity. Fix: give both columns headings that name what is in them (for example "Opening hours and sailings" and "On board"), and move the card sentence to whichever section deals with tickets. Kind: defect. Weight: major. It sends the reader to the wrong place for the one practical fact the heading promises.

**What's working.**
- The grid is clean and consistent. Margins are 120 px on both sides, the two columns are 480 px wide with an 80 px gutter, and the title, the right heading and both rules start exactly on the column edges. Nothing nearly misses an edge, so the page looks built rather than placed.
- Spacing shows the groups. The heading sits about 10 px above its text, paragraphs have about 14 px extra between them, and the title has about 50 px below it. Each level of grouping is clear at a glance.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Both columns end in a light rule at y≈585 with nothing below it, followed by about 215 px of empty page. Either more content (a timetable, a footer) didn't load, or the rules close off nothing. Check in a live browser. If nothing follows them, remove the rules or put the content they introduce under them. Also check how the two columns reflow on narrow screens.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (lines in neighboring columns share baselines; only related elements look alike)

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line?** In the right column, the first paragraph ends with "thirty-five." alone on its last line (about x 680–770, y 292). The second paragraph ends with "bags." alone (about x 680–722, y 414). Each leaves a one-word line with a white gap after it. The two right-column paragraphs look like they trail off, and the column's rhythm is weaker than the left one, where every last line has several words. Bringhurst (*The Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.4.2) says a paragraph should not end on one short word. Fix: pull a word down with a non-breaking space, or use `text-wrap: pretty` on the web. A small rewrite would also work. Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **The subhead says something the text doesn't (copy; no checklist line).** "Fares and cards" (x 680–863, y 135–160) sits over paragraphs about crossing times and wind, bicycles, prams and wheelchairs, and dogs. None of it is about fares or cards. The only mention of cards is the season card, and that's in the left column (y 226). A passenger who scans for prices reads the heading, finds no prices, and stops trusting the page's labels. The left column has no heading at all, so the page has one signpost and it points the wrong way. Fix: put the fares and card details under this heading, or retitle it to match the text, for example "On the crossing". Also give the left column its own heading, for example "Opening hours and sailings". Defect. Weight: major.
3. **A "timetable" with no times (copy; no checklist line).** The title "Winter timetable at the harbour" (y 60–100) promises departure times. The text gives only "every ninety minutes" and "the first crossing", and never says when the first boat leaves. A passenger can't plan a trip from this page, and that's what the title says the page is for. The empty band under the rules (y 585–800) may be where a table was meant to go. If so, that's a layout or loading question; judged as text, the piece doesn't deliver what its title names. Fix: give the actual departure times, at least the first and last sailing of each day. Or retitle the page as winter information if the times live somewhere else. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The body text sets well. It uses one serif family at about 18 px in near-black on white. Lines run about 50 to 57 characters, inside Bringhurst's 45 to 75, and the open leading suits that measure. The two columns read comfortably.
- Paragraphs are marked by space only, with no indents and nothing doubled up. They're short, three to five lines each, so the page is easy to skim.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs and columns break cleanly)

First read: the eye goes to the bold black headline, then down into two grey-black text columns. It reads as a plain informational page from a harbour or ferry office, calm and quiet. I'm assuming it is a public information page that passengers read to plan a crossing.

Walk, Color (Bash was refused, so I judged from the whole image, which is about one screen at 1280 px wide):
- Small palette: yes. It uses only neutrals: off-black text, white ground and light grey rules.
- Saturated color kept to a small area: yes. There is no saturated color.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Near-black text on white, so the structure survives in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. There are no hues to judge.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. Body text, heading and rules are each the same tone in both columns.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not shown by color alone: yes. Nothing is coded by color.
- Dark theme background: yes. This is a light theme.

No line was answered no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The text is a soft near-black on white rather than pure #000. That keeps strong contrast for long reading without the glare of pure black, and it should be kept. The two rules at about y=585 (x 120–600 and 680–1160) are a pale grey that is clearly lighter than the text. They divide the page without competing with the words.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
